m.cycle.name: Season plan: build and taper
m.cycle.short: Planned backwards from race day: a 10-day taper, before it an 8-week build.
m.cycle.plain: Once you set an A race, the app plans backwards from race day: the taper before the race, the build before that, base the rest of the time. A B race does not change the phases; it only gets a short taper.
m.cycle.where: The season plan and every week of the automatic schedule.
m.cycle.calib: Not calibrated: the lengths are rules; the taper days and the transition weeks can be changed in the schedule preferences.
m.cycle.est: Opening a 21-day taper to ultras, and which of two close A races gives way, are estimates.
m.cycle.f1.v: 10 days, the middle of the 8–14 days two meta-analyses found best; 7 days for a 2–3 day Taiwan's 100 Peaks (Baiyue) trip, 10 for a longer one; up to 21 days for a marathon or an ultra in the schedule preferences
m.cycle.f2.v: 8 weeks before the taper, 2 of them recovery weeks; the same as Uphill Athlete's intro-to-ultra plan (8 weeks specific + 2 weeks taper) and inside the ranges of Pfitzinger, Canova, Daniels and Yen-Ching Chiang
m.cycle.f3.v: After the recovery, 3 weeks of easy running by default (0–4 weeks, at most 6 after an ultra or longer); shortened when it reaches the next A race's build
m.cycle.f4.v: No intervals in the 5 days before it, no tempo run or long run in the 4 days before it
m.recovery.name: Recovery after a race, and the descent
m.recovery.short: Recovery by the race's size; one more level when it descends far more than you trained.
m.recovery.plain: After an A race you first recover, then build the volume back up. The bigger the race, the longer the recovery; descending damages the muscles more than climbing, so a race with far more descent than you trained recently gets one more level.
m.recovery.where: The recovery and rebuild weeks of the season plan.
m.recovery.calib: Partly: the recovery days are not calibrated; the descent check compares the race's descent with your recent runs.
m.recovery.est: The race size cut-offs, the descent thresholds and the rebuild shares are estimates.
m.recovery.f1.v: Short and medium 7 days; marathon-size 7 days + 1 rebuild week; ultra 14 days; 100-mile 14 days + 2 rebuild weeks
m.recovery.f2.v: By predicted time (2 / 4 / 6 / 20 hours) or effort distance (21 / 42 / 60 / 160), not by horizontal km alone
m.recovery.f3.v: The race's downhill impact ÷ your biggest single run of the last 6 weeks (weeks 6–9 counted less and less) ≥ 1.5 → one size up; ≥ 1 → no hard session and no descending in the first 3 days after the race
m.recovery.f4.v: The Recovery volume is 40 % of the 4 weeks before the taper; the rebuild goes from 50 % back to 75 %
m.zones.name: Intensity zones: 13 coaching systems aligned
m.zones.short: Coaches name their zones differently; as a share of the lactate threshold they are the same lines.
m.zones.plain: Daniels' T, Friel's Z4 and 80/20's Z3 have different names but all sit near the lactate threshold. With 13 zone systems converted to a percentage of the lactate threshold, the schedule's intensities mean what these coaches mean; at the easy end people differ a lot, so your measured AeT (aerobic threshold) is a second anchor.
m.zones.where: Each session's intensity in the schedule, the heart rate and power zones, the targets sent to your watch.
m.zones.calib: Partly: LTHR, AeT and CP come from your tests and records; the zones' percentages are not calibrated.
m.zones.est: Converting a percentage of maximum heart rate to one of LTHR is off by about ±3 % (one standard deviation), up to ±10 % for some people.
m.zones.f1.v: % of LTHR ≈ % of maximum heart rate ÷ 0.90
m.zones.f2.v: About 0.88–0.92 × LTHR on average, but people differ a lot, so the easy-run ceiling uses your measured AeT first
m.zones.f3.v: Automatic by default: COROS's six zones as percentages of LTHR (< 80 / 80–90 / 90–95 / 95–102 / 102–106 / > 106 %) when the LTHR is believable, else the heart rate reserve or maximum heart rate model
m.zones.f4.v: The charts' heart rate zones default to Friel's seven zones as percentages of LTHR; power zones are percentages of CP (Palladino)
m.load.name: Training load, chronic load and acute load
m.load.short: Daily load averaged over 42 and 7 days shows fitness and fatigue.
m.load.plain: Each session's training load comes from its intensity and duration; each day's load averaged with exponential weights over 42 and 7 days gives the chronic load and the acute load, and their difference is the load balance.
m.load.where: The overview's Training load chart, the automatic schedule's guardrails on adding load.
m.load.calib: Not calibrated: these are published definitions.
m.load.f1.v: The fourth root of the mean fourth power of the 30-second rolling average power
m.load.f4.v: Exponentially weighted averages of the daily load, time constants 42 / 7 days; Load balance = the previous day's chronic load − acute load
m.ramp.name: How fast the chronic load may rise
m.ramp.short: When the chronic load rises too fast in a week: threshold sessions only, then no intervals.
m.ramp.plain: Fitness has to grow slowly. When the chronic load rises too much in a week, the schedule drops the advanced intensity sessions first; when it rises more still, it drops the intervals too. The lines follow Joe Friel's advice on weekly increases.
m.ramp.where: The automatic schedule's intensity sessions, the status card's warning on adding load.
m.ramp.calib: Not calibrated; the lines are relative, so they hold whichever way the load is computed.
m.ramp.est: Turning Friel's 5–8 per week (suggested) / 10 (ceiling) into shares is an estimate.
m.ramp.f1.v: Δ = today's chronic load − that of 7 days ago; c = the chronic load 7 days ago
m.ramp.f2.v: Δ ≥ max(3, 10 % × c): threshold sessions only
m.ramp.f3.v: Δ ≥ min(10, max(5, 15 % × c)): no intervals
m.ramp.f4.v: Base max(2, 5 % × chronic load), Build max(2.5, 7 % × chronic load)
m.cp.name: CP (critical power) and the power–duration curve
m.cp.short: How long you can hold a power is fixed: whatever is above CP comes out of W′.
m.cp.plain: Below CP (critical power) you can go for a long time; whatever is above CP comes out of a limited "battery", W′, and when it is empty you cannot hold on. The whole curve is fitted to your best power at each duration over the last 90 days.
m.cp.where: Reading CP tests, the power targets of intervals, finish estimates when you have a power meter.
m.cp.calib: Yes: the curve itself is fitted to your best efforts; not used without a power meter.
m.cp.f2.v: Short durations are dominated by an anaerobic term that falls with time; long ones level off near CP and fall slowly beyond the sustainable duration
m.cp.f3.v: Modelled threshold power, Anaerobic capacity and the sustainable duration all come from the fit
m.aet.name: AeT (aerobic threshold) drift test
m.aet.short: A steady run: how far the heart rate (HR) drift goes in the second half finds your aerobic threshold.
m.aet.plain: Run steadily at one intensity and compare power ÷ heart rate in the two halves. A small (HR) drift means the intensity is below the aerobic threshold; a large one means you started too high.
m.aet.where: The AeT test, the easy-run intensity ceiling, how the weekly climbing target rises and falls.
m.aet.calib: Partly: the test's bands are not calibrated; how the everyday runs' (HR) drift is cut (how much of the start to drop, how long the tail is, five items) is calibrated with your records.
m.aet.est: Starting 5 beats lower next time after a drift over 5 % is an estimate (Uphill Athlete only says to start lower).
m.aet.f1.v: A steady run after the warm-up, at most 60 minutes of it; power ÷ heart rate of the two halves (pace ÷ heart rate without power)
m.aet.f2.v: < 3.5 %: below AeT (start 5 beats higher next time); 3.5–5 %: the first half's heart rate is your AeT; > 5 %: you started above AeT
m.aet.f3.v: At least 40 minutes after the warm-up; a last 10 % more than 5 % faster than the rest does not count
m.heat-hr.name: Heat and your heart rate
m.heat-hr.short: In the heat the same power takes a higher heart rate; your records show how much.
m.heat-hr.plain: The hotter and more humid it is, the higher your heart rate at the same power. Your runs on the same route in different weather show how many beats each unit of heat load adds for you.
m.heat-hr.where: The heat correction of heart rate, the trail heart rate pace model, the heat acclimation status.
m.heat-hr.calib: Yes: the heat coefficient β is fitted to your route efforts (at least 30, spanning at least 40 units of heat load).
m.heat-hr.est: Without enough records β is 0.3 beats per unit; heat acclimation is shown but does not reduce the heat penalty unless your heart rate shows it working. Both are estimates.
m.heat-hr.f2.v: Heart rate ~ route + power + moving time + time of day + β × (x − 120), shrunk toward 0.3
m.heat-hr.f3.v: A hot session: S += 0.214 × dose × (1 − S), dose = min(1, hot minutes ÷ 60); without one, S × (1 − 0.025) each day
m.hrmax.name: Maximum heart rate from age
m.hrmax.short: Only without a measured maximum heart rate: 208 − 0.7 × age.
m.hrmax.plain: Your maximum heart rate comes from what you entered, your watch or your runs; only when none of them has one is it estimated from age, and it is always marked as an estimate.
m.hrmax.where: The maximum heart rate zone model, data checks.
m.hrmax.calib: Not calibrated: a measured value replaces it.
m.hrmax.est: A value from age is always marked as an estimate.
m.trail-hr.name: Trail heart rate pace model
m.trail-hr.short: A trail race's time from how far you get at a heart rate; the longer the race, the lower the heart rate.
m.trail-hr.plain: A trail race's finish time does not come from power but from how your heart rate relates to your speed in trail running: at a given heart rate, how much effort distance you cover in an hour. The longer the race, the lower the heart rate anyone can hold, so the whole race's time is solved together with its length.
m.trail-hr.where: The race calculator's moving time for a trail race; the home page waterfall's flat layer.
m.trail-hr.calib: Yes: the speed is fitted to your trail runs of at least 45 minutes with heart rate over the last year; the full-effort heart rate curve to your earlier races and full-effort runs, staying near the prior when there are few.
m.trail-hr.est: The whole model is marked as an estimate; converting the prior curve from shares of maximum heart rate to shares of LTHR is an estimate.
m.trail-hr.f1.v: x = moving average heart rate ÷ that day's LTHR (first moved to heat load 120 with your heat coefficient)
m.trail-hr.f2.v: v₀(x) = a + b·x, least squares over at least 6 trail runs
m.trail-hr.f3.v: x*(T) = x₀ − s·ln T; the prior passes 1.00 at 0.5 h, 0.90 at 3 h, 0.85 at 12 h
m.trail-hr.f4.v: T = E ÷ ( v₀(f·x*(T)) · D̄(T) ); E is the effort distance, f the effort you choose, D̄ the mean of the long-race fatigue
m.effort.name: Climbing as effort distance
m.effort.short: 100 m of climbing counts as 1 km at first, then your records fit your own ratio.
m.effort.plain: How much flat running is 100 m of climbing worth? First ITRA's and UTMB's convention, 1 km for every 100 m of climbing, then your own number fitted to your runs of the last year.
m.effort.where: The trail heart rate pace model's effort distance, the home page waterfall's + climbing, race size.
m.effort.calib: Yes: the calibrated item "climbing conversion", used once you have at least 8 runs.
m.effort.est: 1:100 is an organisers' convention without a physiological derivation; how strongly it pulls toward the default and the minimum number of runs are estimates.
m.effort.f3.v: Your runs of the last year, least squares with the flat setting the speed and the climbing its cost; w = n ÷ (n + 10) toward the default, kept within 50–300 m
m.terrain.name: Terrain
m.terrain.short: On technical or scrambling ground the same heart rate covers less effort distance.
m.terrain.plain: On scree, technical trail or ground where you use your hands you are much slower at the same gradient and heart rate. A route marked "mostly technical" or "scrambling" multiplies its effort distance; the more runs you mark, the more the multiplier is yours.
m.terrain.where: The race calculator's terrain choice for a trail race, the home page waterfall's + terrain.
m.terrain.calib: Yes: each level uses the median of "actual ÷ predicted" over the trail runs you marked, pulled toward the prior (worth 2 runs).
m.terrain.nosrc: No published figure was found. The prior comes from one measured run: 15–25 % slower at the same gradient over the whole route, 40 % on the scrambling part.
m.durability.name: Long-race fatigue
m.durability.short: After an hour, a little slower each hour at the same heart rate, levelling off at 80 %.
m.durability.plain: After the first hour you get slower at the same heart rate. The model takes δ off each hour until you reach 80 % of the start and then stops: in long races the speed levels off after falling so far.
m.durability.where: The trail heart rate pace model, the home page waterfall's + long-race fatigue.
m.durability.calib: Partly: your δ is measured but used only when it makes the back-test better; the 80 % floor is not personal.
m.durability.est: Back-tested on 7 trail races: with it the median error is 7.6 %, without it 5.5 %, so it stays marked as an estimate.
m.durability.f1.v: v(t) = v₀ · max(0.80, 1 − δ·(t − 1)⁺), t in hours
m.durability.f3.v: 0.05 per hour (CP falls 9–11 % after 2 hours of heavy exercise)
m.durability.f4.v: A regression within each run of 2 hours or more (the order of the terrain taken out), pulled toward the prior by n ÷ (n + 3); the prior is kept unless the leave-one-out error goes down
m.heat.name: Race-day weather (heat)
m.heat.short: Heat load from air temperature and dew point, each section at the hour you reach it.
m.heat.plain: When it is hot and humid, the same pace takes a higher heart rate and you can hold less power. The heat load comes from air temperature plus dew point, and each section uses the forecast for the hour you get there.
m.heat.where: Every section of the race calculator, the home page waterfall's + race-day weather.
m.heat.calib: Partly: the heat penalty formula is fixed; the trail heart rate pace model uses your heat coefficient β.
m.heat.est: The heat correction by section and hour is marked as an estimate; forecast temperatures are not corrected for altitude.
m.heat.f4.v: Start + the sections before + stops + half of this one; when the times change the weather changes too, recomputed until the cumulative time moves less than 1 second (at most 8 passes)
m.heat.f5.v: Heat does not add time directly; it lowers the heart rate you can hold by β × (x − 120)
m.altitude.name: Altitude
m.altitude.short: The higher, the thinner the air and the slower; acclimatised or not uses different curves.
m.altitude.plain: The higher you go, the lower the air pressure and the less power and speed the same effort gives. Each section uses its own mean altitude; acclimatised and unacclimatised runners use different curves.
m.altitude.where: Every section of the race calculator, the home page waterfall's + altitude, Taiwan's 100 Peaks (Baiyue).
m.altitude.calib: Partly: not for running races; for Taiwan's 100 Peaks (Baiyue) your own altitude slope, pulled toward −6.3 % per 1000 m by its precision.
m.altitude.est: Partial acclimatisation as the midpoint of the two curves and the width of the Baiyue altitude slope are estimates.
m.altitude.f3.v: The midpoint of the two; above 2800 m Bassett's two curves as a cross-check
m.altitude.f4.v: M = 1 − (A training − A race) − (H race − H training) ÷ 100, H the heat penalty
m.grade.name: Energy cost of gradient
m.grade.short: What each metre up or down costs, as the equivalent flat distance.
m.grade.plain: Each metre uphill costs more than on the flat, a gentle downhill saves effort, and a very steep descent costs more again. Minetti's measured curve turns each section into its flat equivalent and decides how the race's time is shared out; walking the steep climbs and how you run the descents only change that sharing, not the total.
m.grade.where: Section paces with power, how the trail model shares the time between sections, the energy for fuelling.
m.grade.calib: Yes: one bin per 2 %, fitted to your 100 m running windows and pulled toward the prior.
m.grade.est: The 0.9 floor on descents is an estimate; running power above 8 % and below −2 % is not validated yet.
m.grade.f3.v: RE₀(g) = RE flat × Cr(0) ÷ Cr(g), never below 0.9 downhill
m.grade.f4.v: Each bin pulled toward the prior by n ÷ (n + 30)
m.hike.name: Hiking speed
m.hike.short: Walking speed changes exponentially with gradient, fastest on a slight descent.
m.hike.plain: Tobler's hiking function: you walk fastest on a slight descent and slower the steeper it gets either way. It is the starting point for walking speed and the cap on Baiyue descents, corrected with your own walking records.
m.hike.where: Taiwan's 100 Peaks (Baiyue) and hiking times, the downhill speed cap.
m.hike.calib: Yes: each gradient bin from your solo hikes and steep sections, pulled toward Tobler.
m.hike.est: The personal fit is an estimate.
m.hike.f1.v: v = 6 · e^(−3.5·|g + 0.05|) km/h, g the gradient
m.hike.f2.v: At most c × Tobler(g), c = the 75th percentile of speed ÷ Tobler on your descents of −10 % or steeper
m.pack.name: Pack weight
m.pack.short: Energy cost of pack weight, gradient and speed, for Taiwan's 100 Peaks (Baiyue).
m.pack.plain: The heavier the pack, the steeper the slope and the faster you walk, the more energy it takes. Multi-day Baiyue trips use this equation to work back from your energy use at the aerobic threshold to how fast you can walk with the pack.
m.pack.where: Multi-day Taiwan's 100 Peaks (Baiyue) trips, steep power hiking conversions, Baiyue fuelling.
m.pack.calib: Partly: the pack weight is the one you recorded; without one, 13 % of your body weight.
m.pack.est: Body weight × 13 % and 0.7 kg of food eaten each day are estimates.
m.pack.f1.v: M = 1.5W + 2.0(W + L)(L ÷ W)² + η(W + L)(1.5V² + 0.35VG) (watts); W body weight, L pack weight (kg), V speed (m/s), G gradient (%), η terrain factor
m.pack.f2.v: Your energy use at the aerobic threshold first, then the speed at which M equals it
m.pack.f3.v: The equation holds for climbs and the flat only; downhill uses the weight ratio (W + L₀) ÷ (W + L)
m.riegel.name: Race distance conversion
m.riegel.short: The longer you run, the lower the power: a power law moves a result to other distances.
m.riegel.plain: The power you can hold falls roughly as a power law of time. Without a CP, your latest road race is converted to the target distance; with a CP it gives the power for races longer than the sustainable duration.
m.riegel.where: Finish estimates without a CP, the sustainable power over long races.
m.riegel.calib: Partly: k is −0.07 by default and fitted to your races when there are enough.
m.riegel.est: A finish time estimated this way without a CP is marked as an estimate; one race to another distance is off by about ±5–8 %.
m.riegel.f1.v: P(t) = CP · (t ÷ TTE)^k, k = −0.07 by default
m.riegel.f2.v: t₂ = t₁ · (d₂ ÷ d₁)^(1 ÷ (1 + k)); with k = −0.07 the exponent is about 1.075
